title: What does Learning Look Like in Action? - 1
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton opens a new run of posts by asking whether learning can actually be seen in a classroom, since there is little point looking for it without agreeing what to look for. He compares teachers to Piaget, who could only infer what was happening inside children's heads from close observation, whereas neuroscientists have scanners. His argument is that waiting for test or exam results is too late, cannot separate school influence from tutors and parents, and may reward students who were already good enough. Existing classroom visit protocols, he says, mostly tick off teacher behaviours, which gives evidence about teaching rather than learning, and busy leaders default to them because they save brain energy. He argues that schools need a doable, low-energy observation framework focused on learning in real time, and previews a four-part protocol to be introduced next.
points: Close observation remains the most powerful tool teachers and leaders have for judging learning, provided it rests on a good protocol.
Test and exam results arrive too late, cannot show who caused the learning, and do not prove students improved.
Typical checklists of teacher behaviours are easy to complete but measure teaching, which is not the same as learning.
Leaders and teachers who have never worked where learning was the central idea will find ticking boxes or waiting for results normal because of their own repeated experiences.
A usable protocol must work in the messy real time of classrooms and link neuroscience insights with what can actually be seen.
quotes: Despite all of the technology now available to neuroscientists, for those of us in the messy world of classrooms, schools and other organisations, close observation is still the most potent tool available to us, providing we have a good enough protocol on which to base our observations.
First, because if we find out that learning hasn’t been happening, it is too late by then to do much about it.
Third, because good test and exam results don’t tell us that students have got better. They might have been good enough already.

Ticking off a simple checklist of teacher (or worker) behaviours saves one heck of a lot of energy. But it doesn’t give us evidence about learning. It gives us evidence about teaching which, as we know, is not the same thing.
But just as sitting in rows didn’t guarantee good learning, neither did being active.

If we want to do right by our students and our children, if we are going to know whether learning is taking place, we have to have an idea of what it looks like as it is happening and then have a framework around which we can marshal our reflections and our decision making.
